questions.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-5x+3?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

${x}^{3}$
${x}^{2}$
${x}^{1}$
${x}^{0}$ 

 
$1$
$1$
$1$
$-5$
$3$

 

$↓$
$1$
$2$
$-3$

 

$1$
$2$
$-3$
$0$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}+2x-3,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}+2x-3).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-1)(x+3)(x-1) \\  & =(x+3)(x-1{)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)=7{x}^{3}+42{x}^{2}$ have multiplicity $2?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. 

For this polynomial, we can factor by noting that the greatest common factor of $7{x}^{3}$ and $42{x}^{2}$ is $7{x}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =7{x}^{3}+42{x}^{2} \\  & =7{x}^{2}(x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $x$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x+6)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-6$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)=27{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-3x-1$ have multiplicity $1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =27{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-3x-1 \\  & =9{x}^{2}(3x+1)-(3x+1) \\  & =(9{x}^{2}-1)(3x+1) \\  & =(3x-1)(3x+1)(3x+1) \\  & =(3x-1)(3x+1{)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $(3x+1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-\frac{1}{3}$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(3x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=\frac{1}{3}$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=\frac{1}{3}$ has multiplicity $1.$

questions.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}-25x+125$ have multiplicity $2?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & ={x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}-25x+125 \\  & ={x}^{2}(x-5)-25(x-5) \\  & =({x}^{2}-25)(x-5) \\  & =(x+5)(x-5)(x-5) \\  & =(x-5{)}^{2}(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=4$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+14x-8$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=4$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-4}={x}^{2}-3x+2,
$$

which means

$$
p(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}-3x+2).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-4)(x-1)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-4)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=4$ has multiplicity $1.$
